text.content:
Playing the Game

A drawn blade changes the conversation. A broken bridge changes the journey. The rules help you decide what those changes mean when timing, danger and the choices of several characters meet.

Begin with what your hero is doing. You can use a learned ability, take a universal action, or describe something the situation makes possible. The DA establishes the circumstances and calls for a roll only when uncertainty has consequences.

Resolve an action

When you use an ability, declare it before rolling. Read its requirements, choose its targets and any printed options, and check range and equipment. Spend the action and any required cost. Roll its attribute if instructed, then apply the complete Weak, Standard or Strong outcome. Finally, record conditions and continuing effects.

An outcome is complete: do not add the Weak damage to the Standard damage. If a Strong outcome includes an earlier benefit, it says so. Instant damage happens once; a condition applied by that damage follows the condition's own timing.

A no-roll ability still costs its printed action. A treatment that takes an hour cannot be completed in one combat turn merely because it is indexed as a Main Action.

Boons, Banes and results

Roll three dice, plus one die for each net Boon or Bane, to a maximum of six dice. With Boons, retain the best three; with Banes, retain the worst three. Add the printed attribute once. Weak is 8 or less, Standard 9–14, and Strong 15 or more.

CircumstanceUsual adjustment
Meaningful help or obstacle1 Boon or Bane
Substantial help or a severe obstacle2 Boons or Banes
Exceptional advantage or difficulty, still possible3 Boons or Banes

These are guides for the DA. They do not turn an impossible attempt into a possible one. Do not count the same obstacle twice under different names. Boons and Banes from distinct valid sources stack, cancel, and then use the three-die net limit.

> Example — keeping the best three. An attack has 3 Boons and 1 Bane, leaving > 2 Boons. Roll five dice. On 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, retain 4, 5, 6 for 15. Brawn +1 makes > 16, a Strong result. If two Banes remained instead, retain 1, 2, 4 for 7; Brawn +1 > would give 8, a Weak result. Neither roll changes the attack's printed damage.

Read retained natural 111 as Weak with an additional complication and 666 as Strong with an additional benefit. The result still makes its printed progress. The DA fits a benefit or complication to the scene; it does not silently double damage or grant another action.

Taking turns

At the start of combat, one player rolls unmodified 3d6. On 12 or more, the player side acts first. Otherwise the opposing side begins. This determines which side starts every round of this combat; do not roll again each round.

The starting side chooses one of its characters to act. Then the other side chooses one. Alternate until everyone has taken a turn. If one side has no characters left to act, the other finishes its remaining turns. A character takes one turn each round. Each side chooses its order as it goes.

On your turn, you have one Main Action, one Maneuver, and movement up to your Speed. You also have one Reaction, available for its stated trigger. Refresh that turn's budget at the start of your turn. A defense roll does not itself spend a Reaction. Choose your retained categories at turn start if Dazed or Grappled.

You can split movement around your actions. You can convert your Main Action into a Maneuver and a Maneuver into another movement allowance. Conversion goes only in that direction. Converting your Main and original Maneuver into movement gives three total movement allowances: a full sprint.

> Example — reaching an ally. Speed 6 lets Mara move 6 squares. She converts her > Maneuver into movement for 6 more, then uses her Main Action to heal a companion. > She has not gained a second Main Action, and any difficult terrain costs still apply.

A Reaction resolves when its trigger says it does, including on someone else's turn. Once spent, it is unavailable until refreshed. A free attack granted by an ability spends no action and may occur more than once in a turn, but free attacks never trigger additional free attacks. Read the granting effect to see which attack it allows.

Attacking and defending

Players roll. When your hero attacks, roll the attack's printed attribute and read its attacker outcomes. This is true even if the target is another player character; the receiving player does not also roll a defense.

When a DA-controlled creature attacks you, roll the defense attribute specified by that attack. It might be Agility to evade a blow, Fortitude to withstand a bodily assault, or another attribute named by the attack. Apply the result from its Weak defense / Standard defense / Strong defense columns. Weak defense is the most dangerous outcome; Strong defense is the least dangerous.

Player's defenseEquivalent attacker outcome
WeakStrong attack
StandardStandard attack
StrongWeak attack

Creature Evasion adds its printed Boons or Banes to your attack. Threat adds its printed Boons or Banes to your defense against that creature's attack. These use the ordinary dice rules; do not add them numerically to the total.

If you control a summon, roll that creature's printed attributes. Its player profile already presents attack outcomes in the correct direction. Your hero's own Brawn or Reason does not replace the summon’s value.

For NPC-only actions, a player or the DA assuming the player role rolls. For an NPC attack against another NPC, roll the defender’s printed attribute and read the attacker’s defense-outcome table. For consequential healing or another task, roll the acting NPC’s attribute. Make one roll; handling dice does not transfer control of the NPC. Off-screen events can use DA judgment.

Damage and resistance

Damage comes from the chosen outcome, not a weapon damage die. Your attribute has already affected the roll; do not add it again to damage. Apply each matching resistance after determining the outcome. Armor DR is physical resistance.

Use the highest applicable resistance of each type, to a maximum of 3. Two sources of physical resistance 2 do not give 4. Physical resistance 2 and Fire resistance 1 can apply together because they protect against different types.

A damaging event always deals at least 1 total damage after resistance. This minimum applies to the event, not separately to every component. It does not create damage for a harmless ability. Conditions, pushes and other riders still apply unless their own rules prevent them.

> Example — steel and flame. An attack deals 3 physical and 1 fire damage. > Physical resistance 2 reduces the physical portion to 1. Fire resistance 1 removes > the fire portion. Take 1 total damage, not one of each type. If both portions had > been reduced to zero, the event would still deal its minimum 1 total damage.

Physical includes impacts, sonic force and supernatural force when the attack says physical. Fire, Cold and Lightning have separate resistances even though their wounds share the Elemental table. Life resistance also reduces ordinary HP healing.

Same-kind numerical bonuses do not add together unless explicitly stated. Conditions with meaningful ratings can add; binary Prone cannot. Boons and Banes use their own stacking rules. Weakness X adds X to its matching damage component before resistance, once per event. Use the highest value of each type, normally capped at 3. It cannot add a damage type absent from the attack. Special vulnerabilities use their printed procedure. Fire Weakness 2 turns 3 fire damage into 5 before resistance; it adds nothing to a purely physical attack.

Shields and guarded positions

Defend is a universal Maneuver that gives 1 Boon to defenses until the start of your next turn. Repeating Defend does not increase that same benefit.

Shield Block spends a Reaction before an eligible defense. While you use the held shield, gain 1 Boon to defenses against attacks the DA judges it can block, until the start of your next turn. Most ordinary physical attacks can be blocked. Defend and Shield Block are separate sources: together they supply 2 Boons. Creatures use shields the same way.

Opportunity attacks

Leaving an enemy's melee reach voluntarily, casting beside it, standing, stowing an item, or retrieving an item can provoke. The enemy may spend its Reaction to make Basic Melee, never a specialty card. Resolve that attack at the start of the provoking action, before the original action takes effect.

Then continue the original action if its actor is capable. Damage alone does not cancel it. An actor reduced to Dying cannot continue. Commit the action on declaration; if interrupted permanently, that action is spent. Additional HP or item costs are paid only when the action continues into resolution. An unspent potion is not drunk by an interrupted character who can no longer act.

Drawing a weapon as part of attacking adds no separate action. Dropping an item is free. Stowing or picking up an item costs a Maneuver. Forced movement never provokes. An ability can explicitly allow movement without provoking.

> Example — a spell under pressure. Vaelis begins casting beside an armed foe. > The foe spends its Reaction on Basic Melee. Vaelis makes the required defense and > loses HP. Still conscious and otherwise capable, Vaelis continues the spell and > pays any remaining printed cost. A healing spell cannot proceed if its upfront > life cost would leave its caster at 0 HP.

Distance, space and cover

All distances use squares. A square is the useful unit for your map; it does not require a fixed conversion into feet or meters. A diagonal step costs one square. Normal ground costs 1 movement; difficult ground costs 2.

You cannot move through an occupied square unless its occupant is Prone. That square costs 2 movement, and you cannot end there. Standing costs 2 movement. An ability that moves you without provoking still respects terrain, occupied spaces and legal endpoints unless it explicitly says otherwise.

A target you must see must actually be visible. An attack also needs a path to it. Partial obstruction gives 1 Bane; heavy cover gives 3 Banes. Heavy cover still leaves a narrow attack path, such as fighting from behind a wall or dense thicket. A solid barrier with no attack path prevents that attack. Concealment that prevents you from seeing a sight-required target is not merely heavy cover.

For a player area attack, choose the printed range, shape, inclusion and exclusions. Roll once using the worst applicable net Boon/Bane situation among its targets. Use that result for all targets; apply their resistances individually. When an NPC area attack affects several players, each player makes their own defense roll.

Push, pull and throw

A push moves a target away; a pull brings it toward the source. Follow a card's specific direction and shape. Apply Stability once to the initial target, reducing the available forced movement, to a minimum of 0. Stability is normally 0; only an explicit grant increases it. Use the highest source, maximum 3.

Spend the entered square's terrain cost from the movement budget. If any positive budget remains, the target enters the final square even if its cost exceeds that budget, then stops. For example, push 1 can enter one difficult square and stop. Stability does not reduce Prone, conditions, voluntary movement, projectile range, obstacle progress or the reduction of a grapple.

A collision with another movable creature forms a moving group. Apply collision damage to the participants using movement remaining on contact, then subtract the new creature's Stability once before continuing. The group moves together; do not charge the same creature's Stability twice in that movement. A hard obstruction stops the group and deals remaining-budget collision damage +1 to each member. The original mover then bounces one square in the opposite direction if possible.

> Example — Stability in a chain. Push 5 strikes Stability 1, leaving 4. After > one normal square, 3 remains. The moving creature strikes a new creature with > Stability 2. Resolve the contact, subtract 2, and use the remaining 1 to move the > group one further normal square. If the attack also inflicted Burning, stopping > the movement would not remove that condition.

> Crowded collisions. Moving groups must finish in separate legal spaces. > If everyone cannot fit, stop at the last position where they can; the DA decides > the arrangement. Placement cannot pass through walls or grant extra forward > movement. The original mover’s backward bounce still applies where possible.

Grappling and capture

Grappling requires a learned ability; it is not automatically granted with Basic Melee. Grappled prevents movement. At ratings 1, 2 and 3, retain respectively two, one or none of Main Action, Maneuver and Reaction, chosen at turn start. The grappler is restricted by their own contribution as well. Multiple grapplers' contributions add on the target. Attacks against a Grappled target gain Boons equal to its rating.

If you still have a Main Action, Force can reduce your grapple by 1/2/3. Grappled 3 needs outside help. A grappler can freely release their own contribution. A grapple is maintained and does not simply decay at turn end.

Attacks are lethal by default. Taking a prisoner requires a printed nonlethal ability, grappling or restraint. Once a helpless captive is secured and no combat remains, return to ordinary narration. You do not need to keep taking turns to conduct a conversation.

Ending a fight

A fight ends when the immediate opposition is resolved, not because everyone decides to ignore an active death roll. Resolve Dying before leaving combat timing. When it is safe to pause and companions can attend to an ordinary fire or similar immediate hazard, settle that hazard as the scene allows. Other conditions remain until their own removal, expiry or remedy. A safe breath restores HP; it does not remove wounds, refund Grit, cure every condition or reverse Last Words.
